transcript.content: Good day. What brings you in today?

Good day, doctor. Well… I suppose I came in because my thinking hasn’t been quite right. Not terrible, I don’t want to make too much of it, but my mind feels foggy lately. At work I’ll be looking at my old cataloguing notes and I can’t seem to keep my place, or I’ll get stuck just deciding what simple thing to do next. I thought maybe I should ask someone about it… if that makes sense.
Have you noticed any changes in your memory or ability to think clearly over the past few months?

Yes… yes, I have noticed that. I don’t want to overstate it, but my mind has felt rather foggy. At work, even with cataloguing notes I’ve used for years, I sometimes lose my place and have to start again. And simple decisions—what to do next, that sort of thing—can feel harder than they should. It’s probably not dramatic, but it’s been enough that I thought I ought to mention it.
Have you noticed any changes in your ability to remember things, solve problems, or follow conversations compared to how you used to be?

Yes… compared to before, I think so. Mostly it’s this fogginess, if that’s the right word. I’ll be at the library with cataloguing notes I’ve known for ages, and I still lose my place or have to go back over them. And even deciding the next simple step can feel oddly difficult. I don’t think it’s disastrous, but it’s not quite like me.
Can you think of specific examples where your thinking has been different lately—like trouble remembering names or events, trouble planning or organizing, or maybe trouble focusing on tasks?

Yes… I suppose the clearest example is at work. I’ll be using my old cataloguing notes—the ones I’ve used for years—and I somehow can’t keep my place. I’ll read a line and then sort of lose where I was, and have to go back over it.

And sometimes it’s not even anything complicated. I’ll be trying to decide what simple thing to do next, and I just… get stuck for a bit. It’s embarrassing, really. I’m not sure if that’s the kind of example you mean, doctor, but that’s what made me think I should come in.
Would you say that these changes in your thinking are noticeably worse compared to how you were, say, six months ago?

Yes… I think I would say it’s noticeably worse than it was. I don’t mean I can’t function, but it’s enough that I came in about it. My mind just feels foggy, and things I used to do almost automatically—like keeping my place in my old cataloguing notes—take more effort now. And sometimes I can’t quite decide what simple thing to do next, which feels… not like me. Is that the sort of change you mean?
Have these difficulties with your thinking interfered with your ability to carry out your usual work or daily activities?

A bit, yes… I mean, I’m still managing, mostly, but things have been piling up more than I’d like to admit. Lecture plans, travel notes, even simple household paperwork—I keep meaning to sort them, and then I just can’t seem to organize myself reliably the way I used to.

It’s not that I don’t care about them. I just lose track of what needs doing first, and then it sits there. I suppose that counts as interfering, doesn’t it?
Would you say these changes in your thinking are a noticeable decline from how you used to function cognitively, or more of a new challenge for you?

I think… it’s more of a noticeable decline, yes. I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is, because I am still getting through things, but it’s not how I used to be.

That’s really why I came in—my mind feels foggy, and even with my old cataloguing notes, the ones I know well, I can’t always keep my place. Or I’ll be trying to decide the next simple thing to do and just… stall. So yes, I suppose it feels like I’m not functioning quite at my usual level. Is that what you mean?
Have you been feeling down, depressed, or have you lost interest in activities you usually enjoy, even a little more than usual?

Yes… a little more than usual, I suppose. I don’t want to overstate it, but most days lately I find myself just sitting at the kitchen table, and everything feels sort of… drained of color.

Even things I normally enjoy—like my old watercolor books—don’t really draw me in. I’ll open one and instead of feeling interested, it just makes me feel heavy. Does that make sense?

Other candidates (F06.81, F32.9, F48.1) are less likely due to the prominence and pattern of cognitive decline alongside depressive symptoms in the context of likely underlying neurodegenerative process.
